stories.headline: Nepal flood death toll climbs as thousands remain missing
stories.dek: Police said 1,344 people are now confirmed dead after an ice-rock avalanche triggered floods and mudslides across northern and central Nepal.
paragraphs: Nepal's flood death toll rose to 1,344 on Saturday as rescue teams recovered more bodies from devastated towns and villages. Police said thousands are still missing. The update matters now because search crews are still working on the eleventh day after the disaster began.

The floods were triggered on August 26 by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border. The surge of water and mud tore through northern and central Nepal. Police said 843 bodies have been recovered intact, while 501 amputated body parts have also been retrieved from flood-hit areas.

Much is still unresolved. Police estimate 4,898 people remain missing, so the death toll may rise further. Authorities said 1,030 bodies have been temporarily buried after DNA collection and other required steps. Rescue teams led by the Nepal Army are still searching damaged settlements and river corridors.
stories.changes: For people in Nepal, this means rescue, identification and burial work will continue, and many families still do not know who survived.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all missing people are confirmed dead, and it does not mean the full scale of loss is known yet.

cover.title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Rises
cover.standfirst: Flash floods and mudslides in Nepal have killed 1,344 people, police said on Saturday. The disaster began on August 26 after an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border. Nearly 4,900 people are still missing, and army-led rescue teams are continuing searches in damaged towns and river valleys.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Show a near-black vertical wall of floodwater, mud and shattered debris driving down a tight Himalayan gorge, seen almost head-on so it fills the upper two-thirds. Carve a stark white channel through the center in the unmistakable silhouette of Nepal — long east-west, with its irregular southern edge and tapering ends — as if the country itself has become the route being gouged out; along the lower edges, let a few tiny Nepali rooflines and a snapped suspension bridge vanish into the surge, while the lower third stays mostly pale, open riverbed and scattered wreckage for type.
art.note: Somber and quiet, in cold grey, brown and muted blue.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a catastrophic flood in motion; a beat later, the white void resolves into Nepal’s map, making the disaster feel like the country being erased from within.

stories.headline: Two survivors found alive 10 days after Nepal floods
stories.dek: A woman was pulled from a mud-buried house and a man from a hydropower tunnel as thousands remain missing.
paragraphs: Nepal rescue teams found two people alive on Saturday, 10 days after flash floods tore through districts near the Nepal-Tibet border. A woman was pulled from a house buried in mud in Nuwakot. A Chinese man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel. Both were flown out by helicopter.

The floods hit Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun and killed at least 1,300 people, according to authorities. More than 5,000 are still missing. Rescue work has centered on hydropower sites, where about 900 workers are unaccounted for and 500 may be trapped in tunnels across 12 projects.

The rescues show some people are still being found, but the scale of loss has not changed. Officials say the disaster was likely caused by a glacier collapse. Teams from China, India, South Korea and the United States are still searching, especially in tunnels and buried settlements.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the search in Nepal is still active and some families still have reason to hope for survivors.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the disaster is easing, because thousands remain missing and most rescue efforts are still focused on mass casualties.

cover.title: Survivors Found In Nepal Floods
cover.standfirst: Ten days after flash floods devastated central Nepal, rescuers pulled one woman from a house buried in mud in Nuwakot and one Chinese man from a hydropower tunnel. At least 1,300 people are dead and more than 5,000 remain missing. Search teams from several countries are still working.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Show the mouth of a Nepal hydropower tunnel in one severe frontal view, split cleanly down the middle. On the left, the arched bore is open with unmistakable ribbed supports receding into darkness; on the right, the same arch is packed solid with engraved layers of mud, rock and broken timbers, and a rescue rope runs into the blockage toward a single tiny white hardhat-lamp glow buried deep inside. Keep the lower third quiet with only the tunnel apron and a thin wash of settled silt, so type can sit across it.
art.note: Quiet, grave, muddy browns and slate greys with a thin cold blue.
art.second_beat: First you read a tunnel open versus shut; a beat later the tiny lamp inside the blocked half reveals that the mountain has closed on someone still alive.

stories.headline: Iran Says U.S. Missiles Hit Oil Tanker Near Kharg
stories.dek: Iranian state media reported a strike on an oil tanker near the country’s main export island after recent U.S. attacks.
paragraphs: Iranian state media said U.S. missiles hit an Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island, a key oil export hub in the Gulf. The United States military had not confirmed any attack. The report came after a wave of U.S. strikes launched in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships and American forces.

Kharg Island is central to Iran’s oil trade, so any strike nearby carries economic and military weight. The latest report sits inside a wider exchange between Washington and Tehran that has already included attacks at sea and strikes on military targets. That raises the risk of further disruption in Gulf shipping lanes.

It is still unclear whether the tanker was badly damaged, whether there were casualties, or whether oil exports were interrupted. Independent confirmation is missing, and the U.S. military has not publicly backed the Iranian account. The next question is whether either side answers with another strike.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this adds to the risk of higher oil prices and more tension around Gulf shipping.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a full regional war is certain, and the reported strike is not yet independently confirmed.

cover.title: Missiles Reported Near Kharg
cover.standfirst: Iran’s state media said U.S. missiles hit an Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island, the country’s main oil export point, on Sunday. The U.S. military had not confirmed the claim. The report followed recent U.S. retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships and American forces. Damage, casualties and any effect on oil exports remain unclear.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Make the upper half a heavy black land-and-sea mass unmistakably shaped as Kharg Island and the surrounding Gulf, with the export channel cut out of it in white so that the void reads, on second glance, as the silhouette of a large tanker hull. From the right edge, a single red missile is already entering that white tanker-shape, not yet exploded; keep the lower third almost empty as flat water for type, with no extra ships, labels, or sky detail.
art.note: Severe and tense; deep navy, black and one hard red-orange accent.
art.second_beat: First you read place; then the hidden tanker appears inside Kharg itself, making the strike about the island’s export function, not just any generic attack at sea.

stories.headline: Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest order over threat case
stories.dek: The Philippine vice president paid 360,000 pesos bail and said she felt unsafe leaving court amid a widening clash with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
paragraphs: Philippine vice president Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a court issued an arrest order a day earlier on three counts of grave threats. The case centers on remarks she made in 2024 about having President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, his wife and another senior official killed if she were killed.

Duterte denies threatening the president and says she was speaking about her own safety. But the case sits inside a deeper break between two political families that ran together in 2022. She is also facing an impeachment trial in the Senate over separate allegations including misuse of confidential funds.

The criminal case now moves ahead while Duterte remains free on bail. If she were convicted, she could be barred from public office and blocked from a 2028 presidential run. It is also unclear how far the Marcos administration will press the case as their political fight hardens.
stories.changes: An ordinary reader should now see that the feud at the top of Philippine politics has become a live criminal case with possible consequences for the next election.
stories.unchanged: This does not remove Sara Duterte from office today, and it does not by itself decide the impeachment case or the 2028 race.

cover.title: Sara Duterte Posts Bail
cover.standfirst: Philippine vice president Sara Duterte left a Quezon City court on Saturday after posting 360,000 pesos bail on three grave threat charges. Prosecutors point to remarks from a 2024 online briefing. She denies threatening President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The criminal case and her separate impeachment trial will now run on.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: At the entrance to a Manila courthouse, show a single waist-high security barrier arm swinging down across the path of a few tiny arriving figures. Draw the barrier so its silhouette unmistakably doubles as a pistol: the curved support reads as trigger guard and trigger, the horizontal arm as barrel, with the courthouse steps and columns reduced to simple blue geometry behind it; keep the lower third mostly open and flat for type. Use federal blue for the court setting and barrier, with one fluorescent pink accent on the moving arm or pivot to catch the eye and mark the moment of descent.
art.note: Tense and public; red, black, and off-white.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a court checkpoint in motion; a beat later the same barrier becomes a gun, turning Duterte’s claim of needing protection and the threat case against her into the same image.

stories.headline: Tesla puts steering wheel-free Cybercabs onto Austin streets
stories.dek: Dozens of gold robotaxis without pedals or steering wheels began running in Austin as Tesla tries to catch Waymo and calm public safety fears.
paragraphs: Tesla on Thursday sent dozens of gold Cybercabs onto Austin streets with no steering wheels or brake pedals. The launch is a bigger test of its driverless taxi plan. Tesla needs a win as car sales and profits have fallen, and investors want proof the business can grow beyond selling cars.

Tesla already runs robotaxis in Texas and Florida, but those cars still have human controls. Waymo is far ahead, with more than 4,000 driverless vehicles in 14 cities. Tesla is also taking a different technical path, relying mainly on cameras rather than adding lidar and radar to help cars read the road.

The main unknown is whether people will trust the service and whether regulators will allow faster expansion. Surveys show most Americans are uncomfortable with driverless cars. Tesla also faces safety investigations in the United States, including probes into crashes, low-visibility driving, red-light incidents and delayed crash reporting.
stories.changes: If you live in Austin, you may soon be able to book a Tesla ride with no driver and no backup controls.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean private Teslas everywhere can now drive themselves legally or safely without close limits.

cover.title: Tesla Cybercabs Hit Austin
cover.standfirst: Tesla put dozens of gold Cybercabs onto Austin streets on Thursday. The new robotaxis have no steering wheel and no brake pedal. Tesla is trying to expand to more cities, but it still trails Waymo, faces safety investigations, and must persuade wary riders to get in.

art.label: Bold symbol
art.concept: Show the gold Tesla Cybercab at a slight front three-quarter angle, nose-first and halfway forced through a standard orange traffic cone that impossibly sheaths most of the car like a too-small safety sleeve. Make the Cybercab unmistakable by its smooth gold body, blunt futuristic front, and visibly control-less cabin with no steering wheel or pedals; keep the background plain and the lower third empty for type, with the cone and car doing all the work.
art.note: Cool, watchful mood; gold car against pale blue-gray city tones.
art.second_beat: First you see a robotaxi emerging; a beat later you realize the whole car is absurdly being contained by a traffic cone, turning the safety-rollout argument into one sharp visual contradiction.

stories.headline: US warns Iranian tanker after strike near Kharg Island
stories.dek: US forces hit one tanker and warned STARK 1 near Iran's main oil export terminal as Brent crude rose above $85.
paragraphs: US Central Command said its forces warned the Iranian oil tanker STARK 1 during blockade operations near Kharg Island, then struck another vessel that did not comply. The action comes days after the US resumed a naval blockade around Iranian ports, saying it was responding to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping.

Kharg Island is Iran's main oil export hub and handles most of the country's crude shipments. The vessel hit was the Curacao-flagged M/T Belma, which US forces said ignored repeated warnings and was disabled with Hellfire missiles. Oil traders reacted quickly because traffic near the Strait of Hormuz affects global fuel supply.

It is still unclear how Iran will respond, whether more tankers will test the blockade, and how long the operation will last. The legal basis for stopping and striking ships will also face scrutiny. Further disruption near Kharg Island could raise shipping costs, insurance rates, and oil prices again.
stories.changes: If you buy fuel or goods moved by sea, this raises the risk of higher energy and shipping costs in the near term.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the Strait of Hormuz is closed or that global oil supplies have stopped moving.

cover.title: US Warns STARK 1
cover.standfirst: US forces warned the Iranian tanker STARK 1 near Kharg Island after disabling another ship that ignored orders, CENTCOM said. Kharg handles most of Iran's crude exports. Brent crude rose above $85 a barrel. Markets now wait to see whether Iran retaliates and whether more tankers are stopped.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Show a tight diagonal convoy of near-identical tanker silhouettes crossing a flat acid-green Gulf, all aimed past a hard black block of Kharg Island near the top edge. One tanker, just off the island and near the centre, is violently broken out of the line: a white impact burst punches through its hull, its body slews sideways, and a few raw marker arcs radiate the warning/strike so the whole shipping flow visibly jolts around a single interdiction. Keep the lower third mostly open acid-green water for type; no labels, no extra detail, just convoy, island, hit.
art.note: Tense and spare; deep navy, rust red, and oil-black.
art.second_beat: First you read a routine stream of oil traffic; a beat later the one ruptured ship makes clear that a single strike near Kharg Island has militarised and disrupted the whole route.

stories.headline: Chinese AI firms push cheaper open models for global reach
stories.dek: Kai-Fu Lee says Chinese labs can compete abroad with models that are slightly weaker but far cheaper to train and use.
paragraphs: Kai-Fu Lee says Chinese AI companies may not need the strongest models to win global market share. In a Bloomberg interview, he argued that cheaper open-weight systems are now close enough in quality to US rivals for many users. That matters as developers and businesses look for lower-cost tools.

Lee said Chinese labs are producing models with about 90 to 95 percent of US capability at a small share of the training cost. He said export controls on advanced chips forced teams in China to use hardware more efficiently. Models from DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen now rank highly on open-source benchmarks.

It is still unclear whether low-cost open models can match US leaders in the most demanding business and research tasks. Benchmark claims vary, and frontier systems still lead in some areas. It is also not clear how tighter US export rules, safety rules, or commercial pressure will affect adoption outside China.
stories.changes: Readers may soon see more cheap AI products built on Chinese open models, especially in apps and services aimed at price-sensitive markets.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Chinese AI has clearly surpassed US AI, or that the most advanced closed models no longer matter.

cover.title: Cheap Chinese AI Spreads
cover.standfirst: Kai-Fu Lee says Chinese AI labs are building open-weight models that reach roughly 90 to 95 percent of US performance at a fraction of the cost. DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen are gaining developers now. The next test is whether low prices can turn benchmark gains into global use.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On pale red seamless paper, place a recognisable high-end server GPU cooler shroud diagonally across the upper half of the frame, tipped so it reads as an emptied shell rather than a hero object. From its open end, a lively spill of many identical cheap USB sticks pours outward and fans across the upper two-thirds, with a few still caught in the lip as if mid-flow; keep the lower third almost bare for type. Light it flat and deadpan so the contrast does the work: one expensive hardware vessel, emptied into a multitude of low-cost portable copies.
art.note: Sharp, public-argument mood; red, blue, black, and off-white.
art.second_beat: First read: costly AI hardware versus cheap distribution; second beat: the valuable thing is no longer the chip itself but the many inexpensive open models escaping from it.

stories.headline: Trump downplays Iran conflict as strikes and diplomacy continue
stories.dek: He called the fighting "small potatoes" even as the U.S. weighed another strike, pushed a U.N. referral, and approved a $5 billion Saudi arms sale.
paragraphs: President Trump said the conflict with Iran was minor for the United States, while also warning that U.S. forces could strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site soon. His comments came as Iranian media reported explosions near Kharg Island and Western powers prepared a new push at the U.N. nuclear watchdog.

The fighting began after U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear sites earlier this year. Vice President JD Vance said he would not call the conflict a war and said major combat had ended after about six weeks. Trump publicly used both terms, calling it a military conflict and also a war.

It is still unclear whether the U.S. will launch another strike, whether Iran will answer with more attacks, and whether the IAEA board will vote to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council next week. Even if that happens, Russia and China could block any new U.N. punishment.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the U.S. is still treating Iran as an active military and diplomatic problem, even while officials soften the language.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a full new U.S. ground war has begun or that the U.N. is about to impose immediate new sanctions.

cover.title: Trump Shrugs Off Iran Fight
cover.standfirst: President Trump said Friday that the Iran conflict was "small potatoes" for the United States, even as he threatened a possible strike on Pickaxe Mountain. Iranian media reported blasts near Kharg Island, and the U.S., Britain, France and Germany are preparing a vote next week on referring Iran to the U.N. Security Council.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: On a stark white cover, place a single U.N. Security Council gavel off-centre and caught mid-swing, angled down toward the lower right, with ample quiet space across the lower third for type. Strip it to silhouette-level essentials: the handle and striking pose must read instantly as a gavel, but the head is not wood — it is unmistakably a bunker-buster bomb form, cleanly substituted in one piece, so the object reads first as procedure and a beat later as impending strike.
art.note: Tense and spare; muted red, navy, sand, and black.
art.second_beat: First you see a diplomatic gavel coming down; a moment later you realise the blow itself is a bomb, collapsing U.N. referral and U.S. military action into the same act.

stories.headline: Ceasefire near Zaporizhzhia plant allows urgent power line repairs
stories.dek: The pause in fighting is meant to help restore outside electricity to Europe's largest nuclear power plant.
paragraphs: A local ceasefire has taken effect around the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Sept. 5. The pause is meant to let crews repair a damaged power line and restore external electricity to the site. That matters because the plant needs steady outside power for safety systems.

The Zaporizhzhia plant in southern Ukraine is Europe's largest nuclear power station. It has repeatedly lost outside power during the war and has had to rely on backup systems. Even when reactors are not generating electricity, the site still needs power to cool nuclear fuel and run essential equipment.

It is not yet clear how long the ceasefire will hold, how quickly repairs can be completed, or when a stable external supply will be fully restored. The wider war around the plant has not ended. Any new shelling, damage, or technical fault could again put the facility under pressure.
stories.changes: For nearby residents and anyone following nuclear safety, the immediate risk falls if outside power is restored and backup systems are used less.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the plant is back to normal or that the fighting around southern Ukraine has been settled.

cover.title: Ceasefire at Nuclear Plant
cover.standfirst: A local ceasefire began near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant on Sept. 5, the IAEA said. The aim is to repair a power line and restore outside electricity to the site. The plant still needs steady power for cooling and safety systems, even when reactors are not producing electricity.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Build a very stripped-down handmade model of the Zaporizhzhia plant on a flat bright-blue card: two unmistakable pale-grey cooling towers and a low reactor block clustered at left, with two thin pylons leading away to the right. Between the pylons, leave a clean, obvious gap where the external transmission line should be; from the far right edge, a tiny orange repair cherry-picker is just entering toward that break, its arm raised but not yet touching. Keep the lower third almost empty blue, with all the action riding the upper half and the missing line doing the work.
art.note: Calm but tense; muted grey-blue palette with one sharp line of electric yellow.
art.second_beat: First you see a nuclear plant and a repair scene; a beat later you realise the subject is the absence itself — the whole danger is one missing outside connection.

stories.headline: Justice Department broadens scrutiny of virus researchers beyond Fauci
stories.dek: A federal inquiry appears to reach past one public figure and into a wider group of scientists tied to pandemic-era research.
paragraphs: The Justice Department is quietly investigating Dr. Anthony Fauci and other virus scientists, according to the summary of new reporting. The effort appears broader than the public fights in Congress. It matters now because Fauci has already become a political target, while federal investigators may be examining a wider set of research decisions and contacts.

Fauci led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases for decades and became one of the most visible public officials during the Covid pandemic. Congressional Republicans have spent years attacking his handling of the crisis and questioning virus research links. A Justice Department inquiry would be separate from those hearings and could reach other researchers beyond government service.

It is still unclear what conduct investigators are examining, how many scientists are involved, or whether anyone will face charges. The full article text is unavailable, so key details are missing. It is also not known whether the inquiry centers on funding, public statements, records, outside collaborations, or some combination of those issues.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means pandemic-era research decisions may face legal review, not just political criticism on television and in Congress.
stories.unchanged: It does not by itself prove wrongdoing by Fauci or any other scientist, and it does not change current medical advice or the basic history of Covid.

cover.title: D.O.J. Examines Virus Scientists
cover.standfirst: A Justice Department investigation appears to extend beyond Anthony Fauci to a wider circle of researchers tied to pandemic-era virus work. The public knows little about its scope, targets, or legal theory. What comes next depends on what investigators were reviewing and whether they found evidence of crimes.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a deep DOJ-blue seamless, stage a forensic dusting in progress: a broad, soft fingerprint brush sweeps diagonally across a row of small clear lab vials, with one vial already behind the brush and several more still ahead of it. Keep the powder arc faint but visible in the air and on the tabletop, and make the vials unmistakably scientific by their shape and caps alone—no labels, no text, no extra props; leave the lower third mostly clean for type.
art.note: Cool, clinical light; muted blues and grays.
art.second_beat: First it reads as crime-scene forensics, then you notice the brush has moved beyond a single vial and is dusting a whole line—scrutiny widening past one figure into a broader set of researchers.
